content.text:
We have T3's comment wording, but nothing enforces it. T3 also has a lint rule that does; inkling doesn't.

**The written rule matches.** The Taste section in our `AGENTS.md` follows T3's: default to no comment, keep one only for a constraint, quirk or invariant, one line where you can and four at most. Both ban restating names, narrating steps and recording history. Ours also bans section labels and TODOs without an issue. Our `// regression: #NNN` test marker is one T3's rule allows too. The only clause we lack is "or explain the fix you just made; the PR carries that." It's worth adding.

**Enforcement is missing.** T3 runs a custom oxlint rule, `oxlint-plugin-t3code/rules/no-low-value-comments.ts`, that rejects:
- comments longer than 4 lines (license headers are exempt)
- section dividers like `// ----` or `// ===`
- test step labels (`// arrange`, `// act`, `// assert`)
- `TODO`/`FIXME`/`HACK` with no issue link
- bare PR or issue numbers (except `regression:` and `quarantine:` markers)
- JSDoc type annotations in TypeScript files, and JSDoc tags with no description
- commented-out code
- a comment that only repeats the name of the declaration below it

Inkling only runs Biome, and Biome can't express this rule. So nothing catches violations in review or CI.

**How far off we are:** I ran T3's rule unchanged against `src`, `electron`, `extension/src`, `packages` and `scripts`, outside the worktree, then deleted the scratch copy. It found 96 problems:
- 81 comments longer than 4 lines
- 15 section dividers
- none of the other checks fired

About 70 of the 96 are in the mascot code, mostly `bot/engine.ts`, `readmeMascot.ts` and its test, `bot/eyefit.ts` and `bot/decor.ts`. The other files have one or two each, such as `notes.ts`, `useSpaces.ts` and `deepLink.ts`.

**If you want real parity, I'd suggest:**
1. Add `oxlint` as a dev dependency with only T3's rule copied unchanged, and run it inside `bun run lint` so CI picks it up. Biome stays as the main linter.
2. Fix the 96 problems in the same PR, by cutting the long comments down to the constraint and deleting the dividers.
3. Add the "don't explain the fix you just made" clause to `AGENTS.md`.

This adds a second linter, which is new tooling, so I haven't changed anything. Do you want me to go ahead?
should we switch to oxlint then?

No, I wouldn't switch completely. I'd add oxlint next to Biome and use it only for the comment rule.

**Why not replace Biome:**
- **Biome also formats our code.** oxlint only lints, so dropping Biome means adopting a new formatter as well. That would reformat the whole repo right after the big refactor and add noise to every open branch.
- **Biome lints our CSS**, including the Tailwind directives. oxlint doesn't lint CSS, so we'd lose that check.
- **Our Biome setup is small and working.** It's the recommended preset plus about 10 tweaks. Moving it to oxlint means matching the hooks rules, the `noLabelWithoutControl` a11y option for `Input`, and the rest one by one, with no gain to users.
- **The only thing we're missing is the custom rule.** Biome can't run it, but oxlint can, and oxlint is fast enough that running both adds almost nothing to `bun run lint`.

**What I'd do:** add `oxlint` as a dev dependency with only T3's `no-low-value-comments` rule turned on and every built-in category off. Then chain it into the `lint` script so CI runs it, and fix the 96 existing problems in the same PR. The config would be one rule file, a small plugin wrapper and a short `.oxlintrc.json`.

A full switch would make sense if we start writing more custom rules, like T3's React effect budget or its test-skip rule, or if we want oxlint's type-aware checks. Until then, a second tool that does one job is the smaller change.

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  changes:
    name: Detect changes
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: read
    outputs:
      frontend: ${{ steps.filter.outputs.frontend }}
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
          # Full history so the path filter diffs the real change set.
          # A shallow checkout can yield an empty diff and silently skip jobs.
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Filter changed paths
        id: filter
        # Pinned to the v4 tag commit: this job gates security checks, so a
        # hijacked floating tag must not be able to falsify filter outputs.
        uses: dorny/paths-filter@ceb8a2b8f2d89434be7ff52d3de7ec3738c5cc9d # v4.0.3

## Checks

| Goal | Command | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Everything | `bun run check` | Bun pin, frozen install (`--ignore-scripts`), typecheck of every workspace, tests, Knip, lint, both builds, ingestion smoke, extension build. CI runs the same steps as separate jobs |

| Tests | `bun test` | |
| Unused code | `bun run knip` | Hard gate in CI; `knip.json` owns entry/project patterns. To clean up locally, run `bunx knip --fix` then `bun install` (re-syncs the lockfile if deps were pruned), fix any `noUnusedLocals` fallout, and re-run `bun run check` |
| Lint and format | `bun run lint` (`bun run lint:fix` to apply) | Biome |
| Bun pin | `bun run check:bun-version` | `.bun-version` vs `packageManager` vs running Bun must agree |
| Extension build | `bun run --cwd extension build` | Builds the Chrome MV3 extension and its service worker |

For early signal, run `bun run check`. `noUnusedLocals` / `noUnusedParameters` are on — the compiler catches dead locals; Knip catches dead exports and dependencies.

None — there are no local hooks by policy. Formatting, linting, and all other gates run in CI.

# sol-loop

This is a workflow for making your code changes more correct before (or
sometimes after) filing a pull request. tl;dr - use OpenAI's GPT Sol to review
your code in a loop.

Make the most minimal possible changes to appease the Sol reviewers. Be careful
of scope creep and don't be scared to push back.

## Budget

- Default: 3 rounds total. Round 1 is full. Later rounds check only
  changed code and open findings.
- Extend to 5 only for security, permissions, auth, data loss, or
  state/concurrency, while a blocker or should stays open with evidence. Or when

  doc, or format-only fixes need no new round.
- One reviewer only. Sol must not start subagents or reviewers.
- Keep a ledger: id, severity, outcome, usage if returned. Never guess it.

## 1. Scope

Run `git status --short`. Do not stash, discard, or include unrelated
changes. Limit review to the change paths if they separate cleanly.
Otherwise stop and ask.

Find the base after `git fetch origin`:

- PR: `gh pr view <n> --json baseRefName,headRefOid`. Check out the branch
  only if clean. Confirm `HEAD` is the PR head, or ahead only by this
  change. Base: `git merge-base HEAD origin/<baseRefName>`.
- Local: `git merge-base HEAD origin/<default-branch>`. No remote: a base
  the user names, or `HEAD` for uncommitted changes only.

The change is base to working tree in those paths, with untracked files.
Use one diff command all rounds. State intent and out-of-scope in 1-2
sentences. Run covering checks. Do not send code this change breaks. Note
missing or pre-failing checks in the brief.

## 2. Start Sol

In T3, call `orchestrator_capabilities`. Pick the latest Sol unless the user
named a version. Do not hardcode an ID. Record provider, model, and effort
only if exposed. Use `delegate_task` every round (`role: "review"`,
`mode: "async"`). Save `taskId`. New `clientRequestId` per round.
`childThreadId` is storage, not the next target. Do not use
`t3_thread_send`, `create_threads`, or `t3_thread_launch` for review.

If T3 tools are not listed, try one direct capability call. Outside T3, use
a native Sol subagent and keep its ID. In Claude Code, use a custom subagent
only if it is set up to run Sol. If no route runs Sol, report the blocker. Do
not substitute a model.

Do not edit scoped files while review runs. Wait for the notice. Do not
poll or start a second reviewer. Timeout, error, or no reply is not
approval. On failure, cancel, verify stop, restart with the ledger.

Round 1 brief (T3 children get no history):

```
Review only. Do not edit, commit, push, comment on PRs, or start subagents.
Repo: <abs path> Base: <sha> Intent: <intent> Out of scope: <scope> Checks: <results>

blocker = intended case wrong. should = real bug callers will hit, in intent. nit = rest.
```

Check each finding and severity yourself. Another path, rare case, or
small cost is a nit, whatever label it came with.

review grew the diff, cut first. Do not agree just to end the loop.

## 4. Next round

Start one only if budget remains and a blocker or should is open, behavior code
changed, or approval does not cover the current behavior diff. Use a fresh

Add `on <effort>` only if verified.

# Babysit PR

Many repos have AI review bots. They're helpful, even if they are not always
right.

## Waiting

Never write your own watcher, polling loop, or `sleep` loop. Use one watcher
per PR: `watch_pull_request` in T3 Code, `pr-wait` everywhere else. Never run
both on the same PR. Every watcher on a GitHub account shares one rate limit.

### In T3 Code: `watch_pull_request`

Handle the existing checks and comments first. Then call
`watch_pull_request` and end your turn. T3 Code wakes you with a message when
a check fails, the required checks pass, someone comments or reviews, or the
branch conflicts.

- **Only the thread that owns the PR watches it.** If you are a delegated
  child task (a reviewer, a Sol round, any `delegate_task` child), never call
  `watch_pull_request`. The parent owns the PR. Do not watch PRs you are not
  working on.
- **A wake is news, not a merge decision.** Check the merge gate yourself.
- **Unwatch when you hand off.** A watched thread stays in Working and out of
  the user's inbox. When you stop (ready, blocked, or asking the user a question),
  call `unwatch_pull_request` first. A merge or close ends the watch on its
  own.
- **"Stopped watching, could not read it"** usually means GitHub's rate limit
  is used up. Run `gh api rate_limit --jq .resources.graphql` before you
  watch again. If `remaining` is near 0, wait for `reset` with one background
  command, then watch again. Never watch again in a tight loop.

### Everywhere else: `pr-wait`

Wait with `scripts/pr-wait` from this skill's directory (use its absolute
path).

```bash
pr-wait <pr> [--repo owner/name] [--until ready|green|any-change]
```

It prints one line per real event. It exits 0 when the `--until` condition is
met or the PR merges, 1 when it needs you (a required check failed, conflicts,
unresolved threads, PR closed), and 2 on bad input.

- `ready` (default): required checks green, Greptile or Macroscope reviewed the
  head, and no unresolved threads. Use this to babysit.
- `green`: required checks only. Use it when the repo has no Greptile or
  Macroscope.
- `any-change`: exit on the first event.

In Claude Code, run it with the Monitor tool (`timeout_ms: 3600000`), so each
line wakes you. Without a monitor, run it as one long command. It ends on its
own.

Start it again after you push, after you handle an exit 1, and after a resume.
It remembers what it already reported, so nothing that arrived in between is
lost. If it says another pid already watches the PR, do not start a second one.
Kill the old one only if its events do not reach you.

With either watcher: when an event needs no action, end your turn without a
message. Never post or say "still waiting".

## GitHub rate limits

`gh pr create`, `gh pr view`, and `gh pr checks` use GraphQL. When GraphQL is
used up, the REST limit is separate and usually still has room. Use
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n>` to read a PR, and
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/check-runs` for checks.

## Reviews

Only act on checks and comments newer than the latest push. Verify every bot
finding against the source before changing code. Fix real findings and CI
failures, distinguish repository failures from infrastructure flakes, and reply
with a written reason when dismissing false positives.

If the repo has `.macroscope/check-run-agents/*.md`, read those rules before you
reply to a Macroscope finding. Its findings cite them.

CodeRabbit is advisory. Treat its findings like any other finding, but never
wait for it and never hold a merge for it.

If a review bot leaves feedback you believe is not worth addressing, reply with
a written reason and resolve the comment. Use the `leaving-pr-comments` skill
for every comment posted on the user's behalf.

Screenshots and videos help as well, when you have a way to upload them.

Keep the PR at the size the user's goal needs. Review loops tend to grow a
PR one cheap-looking fix at a time. Fix real bugs in the intended case.
Decline the rest with a written reason, and list them as follow-ups:
unneeded tests, guards for edge cases that do not matter, extra integration
or compatibility, and small performance costs. Prefer the fix that deletes or
narrows code.

## Base branch and merging

Keep an eye on changes to `main` and rebase when needed. `pr-wait` reports when
new base commits touch this PR's files, and when the PR becomes BEHIND or DIRTY.
`watch_pull_request` reports conflicts only, so check for BEHIND yourself
before you call the PR ready.
If an overlapping PR makes this one obsolete, stop monitoring, report it to the
user, and ask before closing the PR unless closure was explicitly authorized.

If nothing has changed, stay quiet rather than posting filler comments. Stop
when `pr-wait` exits 0, or in T3 Code when the merge gate passes on the latest
head. Merge only when the user explicitly requested it;
otherwise report that the PR is ready. Right before a merge, run `git fetch` and
check the PR again. Never merge when it is BEHIND or DIRTY, or when base commits
that landed after the last green run touch this PR's files. Rebase, push, and
wait for green again.
